transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello. Um, well... I suppose I'm here because I've been having some trouble just... staying in my chair. 

At work—during staff meetings, or even just sitting at dinner—I keep getting up when everyone else is seated. I'll just suddenly feel like I need to refill my coffee, or check a handout, or I'll just walk to the back of the room. Nothing is really urgent, I just... I end up doing that.
Did you experience these feelings of needing to move around frequently when you were a child, or is this a relatively new development in your adult life?

No, I suppose it isn't new. It's... well, it's always been there. Even when I was a girl. 

My mother used to joke that I wore a path between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was ten. And... my old report cards usually said something about it, too. That I was bright, but... I couldn't stay in my seat. Or wait my turn. So... yes. It's been a while.
Aside from the trouble staying in your seat, do you often find that you struggle to maintain focus on tasks or frequently make careless mistakes?

Um, no. Not really. I don't think I have trouble focusing. 

I... I teach, so I grade a lot of papers. You have to pay attention to do that. I haven't really noticed making careless mistakes, either. It's just... what I mentioned before.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others while they are talking or blurting out answers before they have finished asking a question?

Um... yes, I suppose I do that. 

It happens in group discussions... like at my book club, or during curriculum meetings at school. I just... I jump in before someone has finished their thought. The response is already in my head, and I just... blurt it out before I can stop myself.
Do you find that you frequently lose or misplace essential items like your keys, phone, or glasses?
No, I... I don't think so. I usually know where my things are. So, no, I don't really have that problem.
